claims.text: The Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy is derived by removing Co from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
Removing Co alters the lattice-distortion energy landscape.
The altered lattice-distortion energy landscape promotes transient dynamic short-range-ordering clusters.
The Co-free and Co-containing alloys have predominantly solid-solution initial structures.
The interaction of SRO clusters with dislocations depends on temperature and strain rate.
At lower strain rates and higher temperatures, additional deformation time permits SRO clusters to evolve and partially relax.
Evolution and partial relaxation of SRO clusters facilitate dislocation cross-slip.
Evolution and partial relaxation of SRO clusters facilitate dynamic recovery.
SRO-enabled cross-slip and dynamic recovery cause the Co-free alloy to soften relative to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi at lower strain rates and higher temperatures.
At higher strain rates and lower temperatures, SRO clusters form quickly.
At higher strain rates and lower temperatures, SRO clusters act as effective dislocation-pinning sites.
SRO-mediated dislocation pinning increases dislocation density and work hardening.
Relative to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi, the Co-free alloy will have higher yield strength at high strain rates and low temperatures.
Relative to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi, the Co-free alloy will have greater strain hardening at high strain rates and low temperatures.
Relative to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi, the Co-free alloy will exhibit greater softening at low strain rates and high temperatures.
Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi does not exhibit the same dynamic SRO-mediated dislocation behavior as the Co-free alloy.
The proposed hypothesis is bounded to temperatures of 300–500 K and strain rates of 10^-4 to 1 s^-1.
A lack of SRO differences between the alloys, or mechanical differences without corresponding SRO evolution, would falsify dynamic SRO as the controlling explanation.
